passage: The class group buzzed during the lunch break. Sarita opened it and saw herself: the sports-day clip, the moment she tripped at the finish line, slowed down, with a cartoon splat sound added. Under it, forty-two comments. Laughing faces. "Elephant alert." "Earthquake in Andheri." Her face went hot and then cold. She wanted to throw the phone into the dustbin and never come back to school. Instead, hands shaking, she took screenshots of the clip, the comments and the name of the account that posted it. After the last bell she went to Tarun sir, her class teacher, and held out the phone without a word. He read it all, then pulled a chair close. "This is not your fault, Sarita. Not one bit." That same afternoon he reported the post, called her mother, and took the screenshots to the principal's office.

qa.q: What did Sarita take screenshots of?
qa.a: She took screenshots of the clip, the comments and the name of the account that posted it.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel when she saw the clip, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and exposed; her face went hot and cold and she wanted to throw the phone away and never come back to school.

qa.q: Which of Sarita's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Saving screenshots and showing them to Tarun sir the same day gave a trusted adult the evidence to report the post and involve her mother and the principal.

qa.q: How might Tarun sir have felt reading the comments?
qa.a: He was probably angry about the cruelty and protective of Sarita, which is why he told her it was not her fault and acted that afternoon.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who finds a clip shared with cruel comments, feels exposed, and saves evidence and tells a trusted adult, who reports it.

passage:
Mahima knocked twice and pushed the door open. "Gurpreet? Dinner's getting cold. Why are you sitting in the dark?"
"Nothing."
"That's a big nothing. Show me."
He turned the phone. An edited photo of him in his turban, with a crown drawn on and a caption about "the clown of 11C". Two hundred reactions.
"Who made this?"
"Some page. Everyone's sharing it. Maybe I deserve it, I was showing off at the debate."
"No. Listen to me. Nobody deserves this. It isn't your fault." Mahima sat on the bed. "Don't delete anything. Screenshot the page, the comments, the dates."
"If you tell Mummy, it'll get worse."
"I'm telling her now, and we'll do it together. Then we report the page and block it."
They walked out to the kitchen. Mummy read it, put down the ladle and said, "I'm writing to your class teacher tonight." She did, before anyone ate.

qa.q: What did Mahima tell Gurpreet not to do?
qa.a: Mahima told him not to delete anything.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when he said "Maybe I deserve it"?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and helpless, sitting in the dark and blaming himself for showing off.

qa.q: What steps did Mahima lay out, and why do they help?
qa.a: Mahima told him to screenshot the page, comments and dates, tell Mummy, then report and block; this keeps evidence and brings in adults who can act.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt reading the page?
qa.a: She was probably upset and protective, putting down the ladle and writing to the class teacher that very night.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager shamed by an edited photo with cruel comments, who is told it is not his fault and helped to save evidence, tell an adult and report.

passage: It's been two months, so I can look back at it now. On the school trip I fell asleep on the bus, mouth open, and someone took a photo. By the time we got home it was on a meme page with comments I won't repeat. I remember lying on my bed feeling like my skin was inside out. I thought: this is who I am now. My friend Shreya called and said, "Don't reply. Screenshot everything." I did, sniffling. The next morning, well, I almost didn't go. But I went straight to Ms Fernandes, the school counsellor, before first period. She looked at every screenshot slowly and said it was not my fault, that sleeping is not a crime. Within the hour she had the principal and my parents on the phone, and the page was reported. It came down in two days. I, Kalyani, still ride that bus.

qa.q: Where was Kalyani when the photo was taken?
qa.a: On the bus during the school trip, asleep with mouth open.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel lying on the bed that night?
qa.a: Kalyani felt exposed and ashamed, like having skin inside out, and hopeless, thinking this is who I am now.

qa.q: What did Shreya and Ms Fernandes each do well?
qa.a: Shreya said not to reply and to screenshot everything, and Ms Fernandes looked carefully, said it was not Kalyani's fault and brought in the principal and parents within the hour.

qa.q: How might Shreya have been affected by seeing the photo spread?
qa.a: Shreya was probably worried for Kalyani and angry at the page, and relieved when the counsellor took it seriously.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager exposed by a mocking photo who saves evidence, tells a trusted adult and has the page reported, learning it was not their fault.

passage:
"Suraj. It's one in the morning. Why is your face blue?"
"Go to sleep, Sachin."
"You're scrolling again."
Suraj sat up. "Look at this. Anushka, from our batch. Internship in Singapore. Karan got engaged. Pooja's on a beach somewhere. And I'm here, failing thermodynamics, in a room that smells of your socks."
"Hey. The socks are washed."
"You know what I mean. Everyone's ahead."
Sachin propped up on an elbow. "Karan also cried in the corridor about his placement last month. Did he post that?"
"No."
"Pooja posted the beach. Not the fight with her parents to go."
Suraj was quiet. "So it's only the good bits."
"It's always only the good bits. Give me that." Sachin held out his hand. "Phone on my table till breakfast. Deal?"
Suraj hesitated, then passed it over. He lay down and stared at the ceiling fan, heart still racing, but slower.

qa.q: What time was it when Sachin spoke to Suraj?
qa.a: It was one in the morning.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel while scrolling through the posts?
qa.a: Suraj felt behind and inadequate, comparing himself with friends' internships, engagements and holidays while failing a subject.

qa.q: What did Sachin suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Sachin asked for the phone until breakfast, which limits late-night scrolling, and reminded Suraj that posts show only the good bits.

qa.q: How does Sachin see his friends' posts differently from Suraj?
qa.a: Sachin knows the hard parts behind them, like Karan crying about placement, so he sees the posts as highlights rather than whole lives.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who scrolls through friends' news and feels behind, and a friend who reminds him posts are highlights and limits his screen time.

passage:
Looking back, last winter was the worst of it. I had graduated, I was back at my parents' house in Nagpur, sending applications into silence. Every night I would open the photo app and scroll. A school friend's wedding in Udaipur. Someone's first salary treat. Someone's flat with plants. Each one felt like a small slap. By midnight I would be convinced I, Suraj, was the only failure left in the whole batch.
It was my cousin Hemant who said something. We were on the terrace and he'd seen me refreshing. "You know my wedding photos?" he said. "We fought in the car for an hour before those." I laughed, then felt odd.
So I tried something small. The app got a thirty-minute limit, and I stopped opening it after dinner. It didn't fix the job hunt. But my evenings stopped ending in that heavy, sinking feeling. I got a job in March.

qa.q: What limit did Suraj put on the app?
qa.a: A thirty-minute limit, and no opening it after dinner.

qa.q: How did the posts make Suraj feel by midnight?
qa.a: Each post felt like a small slap, and by midnight Suraj felt like the only failure left in the batch.

qa.q: Which choice helped Suraj, and why?
qa.a: Limiting time on the app and stopping after dinner cut down the comparing, so evenings no longer ended in a sinking mood, even though the job hunt went on.

qa.q: How might Hemant have seen Suraj refreshing the phone?
qa.a: Hemant probably felt concerned and understanding, and shared the car fight to show that even happy photos hide hard moments.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who compares himself with friends' posts, feels behind, and helps his mood by limiting time and remembering posts show highlights.

passage:
Mentor's note, second-year counselling hour, Wednesday.
Leela came in for the routine check-in but kept glancing at the phone face-down on the desk. When I asked how the term was going, Leela said, "Fine," and then, after a pause, "Everyone else seems to have their life sorted." Leela showed me the posts: a classmate's paid internship, a cousin's engagement, a friend's trip to the hills. Leela's voice dropped with each one. Leela said the scrolling started after dinner and went on past two.
I asked what Leela's own last week looked like. It included a debate win and helping a friend, Kiran, move hostels. None of it had been posted. We talked about highlight reels, and Leela laughed a little at that. We agreed on one experiment: no scrolling after eleven for a week, and one line a day in a notebook about something real. Follow-up set for next Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Leela's own last week include?
qa.a: It included a debate win and helping a friend, Kiran, move hostels.

qa.q: How was Leela feeling when showing the mentor the posts?
qa.a: Leela felt discouraged and behind, the voice dropping with each post and saying everyone else seemed to have life sorted.

qa.q: What experiment did they agree on, and why might it help?
qa.a: No scrolling after eleven for a week and writing one real thing a day; it limits comparison and reminds Leela of an actual life that isn't posted.

qa.q: How might Kiran see Leela's week compared with Leela's view?
qa.a: Kiran would probably remember Leela as a helpful friend who made a hard move easier, which is far from being behind.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who feels behind after scrolling friends' news and, with a mentor, remembers that posts show highlights and limits screen time.

passage: Shreya, before you press that forward button, let your Saurabh chacha tell you something. I was twenty, in Pune, and phones had just started sending messages to many people at once. One night a message came: the water supply in our area was poisoned, don't drink, forward to everyone. I felt a jolt, I tell you, like I was saving lives. I sent it to forty people. Our neighbour, old Mrs Kulkarni, who lived alone, didn't drink water for a whole day. She fainted on the stairs in the heat. It was all false. Someone made it up for fun. I sat with her at the clinic that evening and couldn't look at her. Next day I went to the municipal office and asked. That was the last time I forwarded anything without checking. You won't feel like a hero. That's alright.

qa.q: How many people did Saurabh send the message to?
qa.a: He sent it to forty people.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel when he first read the message, and later at the clinic?
qa.a: At first he felt a jolt, as if he was saving lives; at the clinic he felt so ashamed he couldn't look at Mrs Kulkarni.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did young Saurabh change?
qa.a: Seeing Mrs Kulkarni faint because of the false message; after that he checked with the municipal office and stopped forwarding anything unchecked.

qa.q: How was Mrs Kulkarni affected by the rumour?
qa.a: Living alone, she believed it, went without water for a day and fainted on the stairs, so a made-up message caused her real harm.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who forwards a shocking message without checking, sees the harm it causes, and learns to pause and check the source.

passage:
Jomon's phone was on four per cent when the message landed in the family group: a blurry photo of a man near their colony gate, and the words "CHILD LIFTER SPOTTED, share urgently". His heart jumped. His little cousins played at that gate. With no time to think and the battery flashing, he forwarded it to three other groups, then the screen went black.
When he got to the hostel charger an hour later, there were forty messages. His cousin Mridul had written, "Jomon, this is Raju bhaiya who sells vegetables. People are shouting at him." Jomon felt sick. He called Mridul, who said a crowd had gathered, and the colony watchman had calmed them down.
Jomon posted in all four groups: "I forwarded without checking. This is false. The man is our vegetable seller. Please delete." Then he messaged Raju bhaiya's son to say sorry.

qa.q: What did the message in the family group claim?
qa.a: "CHILD LIFTER SPOTTED, share urgently", with a blurry photo of a man near the colony gate.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he read Mridul's message?
qa.a: Jomon felt sick with guilt and shock, realising the forward had put an innocent man in danger.

qa.q: How did Jomon try to repair the harm, and what could he do next time?
qa.a: He posted a clear correction in every group and apologised to the seller's son; next time he could pause, especially under pressure, and check before forwarding.

qa.q: What is it like for Raju bhaiya when the message spreads?
qa.a: He is suddenly treated as a criminal by people who buy from him, frightened by a shouting crowd over a photo he never knew was taken.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who forwards a shocking message without checking, sees it harm an innocent man, and corrects it.

passage:
Rekha was halfway through her lunch at the Hyderabad office canteen when the family group lit up. A message with the municipal logo: the tap water in their ward was contaminated, don't drink, stock up on cans. Nani had already replied with three praying hands. Rekha's thumb hovered over forward. Her aunt's family lived in the next ward, with a newborn.
"What's that face?" asked Gurleen, sitting opposite.
Rekha showed her. Gurleen frowned. "The logo's stretched. And 'contaminated' is spelled wrong."
Rekha opened the municipal website. No notice. She searched the ward name. Nothing. She felt a strange mix of relief and embarrassment. She typed in the family group instead: "I checked, there's no notice from the corporation. Please don't forward, it looks fake." Nani wrote back, "Oh! Thank you, beta." Rekha finished her cold rice, a bit slower.

qa.q: What did Gurleen notice about the message?
qa.a: The logo was stretched and "contaminated" was spelled wrong.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling after she found no notice on the website?
qa.a: She felt a mix of relief and embarrassment, relieved it was false and a little embarrassed she nearly forwarded it.

qa.q: What small steps helped Rekha avoid spreading the rumour?
qa.a: Pausing before forwarding, looking closely with a friend, and checking the official website for a notice before posting a calm correction.

qa.q: How might Nani have been affected if Rekha had forwarded the message?
qa.a: Nani, who already reacted with worry, might have panicked more and spread it further; the correction instead brought her relief.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult about to forward a shocking message, who pauses, checks the source and skips the forward.

passage: Gopika, you asked why I never comment on those viral videos. Let your Hansa ma'am, the old hand at this desk, tell you. I was twenty-five, a trainee like you. A clip went round of a bus conductor screaming at a young woman, and within an hour it had thousands of angry comments, his address, calls to get him fired. I felt it too, that burning pull. I typed something nasty. My finger was right there. Then my senior at the time said, "Wait for the full video." I didn't post. Two days later the longer clip came out: the woman had slapped a child and he was protecting the child. The man had already been suspended. His daughter was crying in a news interview. I think about her face often. Nothing I didn't write could hurt anyone.

qa.q: What did the longer clip show?
qa.a: The woman had slapped a child and the conductor was protecting the child.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling while typing the nasty comment?
qa.a: Hansa felt a burning pull of anger, the same outrage everyone else was sharing, and was close to posting.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Her senior saying "Wait for the full video" made her hold back; the full clip showed the story had been partial, so her restraint spared an innocent man more cruelty.

qa.q: How was the conductor affected by the pile-on?
qa.a: He was suspended, his address was shared, and his daughter cried in an interview, so thousands of comments caused real harm to him and his family.

grounding: It illustrates an onlooker who feels the pull to join an online pile-on over a clip, holds back, and later learns the story was partial.

passage:
The flight to Kochi was delayed four hours and the gate was deafening, a cleaning machine on one side, a crying baby on the other. Jomon scrolled to pass the time. A clip was everywhere: a woman in a car park shouting at a delivery rider. Twenty-three thousand comments. Some shared her office name. His colleague Gurleen messaged: "Did you see this?? Disgusting. Tag her office." His thumb twitched. He felt that hot pull, the satisfaction of joining in.
Then he noticed the clip began mid-sentence. He watched it again with the sound up over the noise. Someone off-camera was also shouting. There was no start, no reason given.
He typed back, "Don't know what happened before. Not going to tag anyone." Gurleen sent an eye-roll. Jomon closed the app and bought tea. The board changed again: another hour.

qa.q: How long was the flight delayed at first?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: What did Jomon feel when Gurleen asked him to tag the office?
qa.a: He felt a hot pull and a kind of satisfaction at the thought of joining in, his thumb twitching.

qa.q: What did Jomon notice that helped him hold back?
qa.a: The clip began mid-sentence and someone off-camera was also shouting, so he realised he did not know the full story.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have seen Jomon's refusal?
qa.a: Gurleen seemed irritated or scornful, sending an eye-roll, perhaps feeling Jomon was avoiding taking a side.

grounding: It illustrates a user who feels the pull to join thousands attacking a person over a clip, sees the story is partial and refuses to add cruelty.

passage:
Sharmila was on the office shuttle in Pune when Thomas, her teammate, leaned across the aisle with his phone. "Look at this cab driver. Swearing at a passenger. Everyone's reporting him." The clip had half a million views. The comments were vicious: his number plate, his face circled, jokes about his accent. Sharmila felt the familiar itch. Her fingers were already forming a clever line. People would like it.
She watched it again. The clip was nine seconds long. The passenger was out of frame. Nobody knew what came before.
"You're not commenting?" Thomas asked.
"I don't know what happened," she said. "Neither does anyone in there."
Thomas shrugged. "He still swore."
"Maybe. Doesn't need my voice too." She put the phone in her bag and watched the traffic instead. It felt oddly lonely, and also like the right kind of quiet.

qa.q: How long was the clip?
qa.a: The clip was nine seconds long.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling as she read the comments?
qa.a: She felt a familiar itch, tempted to write a clever line people would like, before she stopped.

qa.q: Why was Sharmila's choice fair?
qa.a: She noticed the clip was short, the passenger was out of frame and nobody knew what came before, so she chose not to add to the cruelty.

qa.q: How does Thomas see the cab driver's clip?
qa.a: Thomas sees it as clear proof, saying "He still swore", and does not feel the need to know the rest of the story.

grounding: It illustrates an onlooker who feels the pull of an online pile-on, sees the story is partial, and quietly refuses to add cruelty.

passage:
"Can you read this before I post it?" Ankita turned her laptop to Lokesh.
"'Thrilled to share that every day at the agency is a new adventure. Grateful for this incredible team.' Ankita, you cried in the bathroom yesterday."
"That's not the point. Recruiters look at the profile."
"I know. But 'every day is a new adventure'?"
"Everyone writes like that." She rubbed her eyes. "Honestly, I'm tired. I spend Sunday planning posts. I smile in every photo. I feel like a brochure."
"Then write something true but still professional. What did you actually learn?"
She thought. "How to handle a client who changes the brief five times."
"Post that. People would read that."
"And the crying?"
"Keep that for me and your sister. Not everything goes online."
Ankita deleted the first line. Her shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: What did Ankita actually learn at work?
qa.a: How to handle a client who changes the brief five times.

qa.q: How does Ankita feel about keeping up her online image?
qa.a: Ankita feels tired and strained, spending Sundays planning posts and feeling like a brochure.

qa.q: What advice did Lokesh give, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: He suggested posting something true but professional and keeping private struggles for close people, so the profile stays honest without exposing everything.

qa.q: What would change if Ankita posted the 'new adventure' line after all?
qa.a: It would add to the gap between her public image and real life, and the strain of performing would probably grow.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional who curates an image for work and followers, feels the strain, and chooses honest posts while keeping some things private.

passage:
Two years ago I started posting my home cooking to get noticed, and it worked a little: four thousand followers, a small brand of spices asking for a collaboration I turned down. What nobody saw was the other side. I, Nitin, would cook a dish three times to get the steam right in the photo. I ate cold dinners. I wrote cheerful captions on days I felt flat. Once my friend Aditi dropped by and I asked her to stand still while I shot her plate. She put her fork down and said, "Are we eating or filming?" That stung, because it was true.
So I changed a few things. I still post, but once a week, and only food I actually cooked for people. I made a second, locked account for eleven friends, where I post burnt rotis. Aditi follows both. She says the second one is funnier.

qa.q: How many friends can see the second, locked account?
qa.a: Eleven friends.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when Aditi asked "Are we eating or filming?"
qa.a: Nitin felt stung and a little ashamed, because the question was true.

qa.q: Which changes helped Nitin, and why?
qa.a: Posting once a week only food cooked for people, and keeping a locked account for friends, kept the public page honest and gave Nitin a private space.

qa.q: What was it like for Aditi when she had to wait for the photo?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt frustrated and a bit hurt, as if the visit mattered less than the post.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who curates a public cooking image, feels the strain of performing, and protects honesty and a private space.

passage:
Supervisor's note, design studio, Friday.
For three weeks Parul has been posting her work every morning on the portfolio site and on two social accounts, each piece with a long caption about "passion". She is good, and the posts are getting her noticed; two recruiters wrote to her. But I noticed she comes in with red eyes, redoes screenshots of the same mock-up four times, and checks follower counts during reviews. On Tuesday she said, half joking, "I have to be the brand now, not a person."
I asked her to lunch today. I said some curation is part of the job, and I do it too. I also said her best piece this year was one she never posted, because it was private work for a small bakery. We agreed she would post twice a week, keep weekends offline, and let Jagdish from the team review captions for honesty, not polish.
Supervisor, P. Nair

qa.q: How many recruiters wrote to Parul?
qa.a: Two recruiters wrote to her.

qa.q: What did Parul's comment "I have to be the brand now, not a person" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt strained and pressured, as if performing online had taken over who she was.

qa.q: What plan did they agree on, and what makes it balanced?
qa.a: Posting twice a week, weekends offline and a teammate reviewing captions for honesty; it keeps some curation for jobs while protecting rest and truth.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see the task of reviewing captions?
qa.a: Jagdish might feel trusted and glad to help Parul sound like herself, while perhaps unsure how blunt to be about honesty.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional who curates her public image and feels the strain, and a supervisor who helps her keep it honest with private time.

passage:
In Palakkad town, the tea shop near the bus stand opened at six, and every Sunday Hafsa was there by seven, her phone left at home on purpose. She had started this in January, after a month where she'd found herself scrolling on the school staff-room bench, on the bus, even at her grandmother's bedside. Now there were rules she kept loosely. No phone before breakfast. Two gossip pages muted, not unfollowed, so she wouldn't have to explain. The school's parents' group stayed on, because that mattered.
Chandrika arrived at quarter past, bringing banana chips. They talked about her student who stammered and was reading aloud now, about Chandrika's mother's knees.
"You're calmer these days," Chandrika said. Hafsa thought about it. She still missed some news. She sipped her tea. "I hear the birds now," she said, and it didn't feel silly.

qa.q: What time did the tea shop near the bus stand open?
qa.a: It opened at six.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel about the changes she had made?
qa.a: She felt calmer and more at ease, though she admitted she still missed some news.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's limits were well chosen, and why?
qa.a: Muting draining pages while keeping the parents' group on protected her calm without cutting off useful connection.

qa.q: How might Chandrika experience the Sunday mornings?
qa.a: Chandrika probably feels valued and close to Hafsa, having her full attention and a real conversation without a phone between them.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who sets phone-free times, mutes draining accounts and keeps real friendships, while staying connected where it matters.

passage:
At nine every night Zanele put her phone in the kitchen drawer of her flat in Johannesburg and shut it with her hip. It was an old habit now, three months old. She had also muted two accounts that made her feel ugly and poor, and one former colleague who posted only complaints. She kept the family group on loud, because her gogo was unwell in Durban.
Tuesday was running night. Kwame waited at the corner of the park, stretching.
"Phone?" he asked.
"Drawer. Well, pocket for now. Emergency only."
They ran two loops under the jacaranda trees, talking about his sister's wedding and her project at work. Afterwards, sitting on a bench, Zanele noticed she wasn't reaching for anything. Her hands just rested on her knees. Kwame nudged her. "You're less jumpy lately." She smiled. "Less noise," she said.

qa.q: What time did Zanele put her phone in the kitchen drawer?
qa.a: At nine every night.

qa.q: What does Zanele's resting hands on the bench suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: They suggest she feels calm and settled, no longer restless to reach for her phone.

qa.q: Why did Zanele keep the family group on loud?
qa.a: Because her gogo was unwell in Durban, so she kept that useful connection open while cutting out what drained her.

qa.q: How has Kwame noticed a change in Zanele?
qa.a: Kwame sees her as less jumpy, and seems glad to have her more present on their runs.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who keeps phone-free time, mutes draining accounts and values in-person friendship while keeping useful family connection.

passage:
The engineering floor at the water utility office went quiet at one o'clock, and Arohi stood up, leaving her phone face-down in her drawer. "Lunch?" she called to Zeenat.
Zeenat raised an eyebrow. "No phone again?"
"The site team can call my desk line. Everything else can wait forty minutes."
It had started after a month of eating at her desk with three chat windows open and never tasting her food. She had muted the office gossip group, but not the incident channel, which mattered. In the canteen they took the corner table by the window. Zeenat told her about her brother's new job in Surat; Arohi told her about the pipeline drawing that finally balanced. They laughed at nothing much. When they got back, there were twelve messages. None were urgent. Arohi answered them in six minutes and felt oddly light.

qa.q: How long did Arohi say everything else could wait?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel after answering the twelve messages?
qa.a: She felt oddly light, relieved that nothing was urgent and that the break had cost nothing.

qa.q: What did Arohi do that protected her attention without cutting off work?
qa.a: She kept her desk line and the incident channel open for real needs, but left her phone and muted the gossip group during lunch.

qa.q: What might lunch be like for Zeenat now compared with before?
qa.a: Zeenat probably feels more listened to, since Arohi is present and talking instead of eating at her desk with chat windows open.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who sets phone-free times, mutes a draining group and keeps real friendship, without losing useful work connection.

passage: I'm Irfan, and on our trip to see family in Naples I watched my little cousin Charu. At the café, a waitress scooped her up and kissed both cheeks. Charu went stiff and twisted to look at Auntie's face. Auntie smiled and nodded. Charu slowly patted the waitress's hair. In Helsinki last week, nobody touched her at all. She kept holding her arms up to strangers.

passage:
Monday: At Nani's house in Delhi, three aunties took turns to cuddle Harish. He pushed at their chins and cried until his mother, Sarika, held him.
Thursday: In a London café, nobody reached for him. Harish held his arms out to a smiling lady. She only waved.
Saturday: An aunty hugged Sarika. Harish watched Sarika laugh, then leaned in too.

qa.q: Where did the three aunties cuddle Harish?
qa.a: At Nani's house in Delhi.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling as she noticed Harish change over the week?
qa.a: Sarika was probably amused and relieved, seeing that Harish relaxed once he saw her laugh.

qa.q: What could Sarika do if Harish cries when relatives cuddle him?
qa.a: She could take him back calmly and let him watch from her lap until he feels ready.

qa.q: How might the lady in London have seen Harish holding out his arms?
qa.a: She probably felt touched but unsure, and waved instead because she was not used to holding a stranger's child.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler who is held by relatives in one place and kept apart by strangers in another, and who takes cues from his mother's comfort.

passage: Vijay, two, had flown from Toronto to Hyderabad to meet his grandparents. In the colony, neighbours grabbed his cheeks and lifted him up. Vijay froze and stared at his papa, Abhinav. Abhinav smiled and said, "It's okay, that's Rao uncle." Vijay's fists opened. By evening he was sitting on Rao uncle's knee, pulling his moustache.

qa.q: What did Vijay do when the neighbours lifted him?
qa.a: Vijay froze and stared at his papa, Abhinav.

qa.q: How did Abhinav likely feel when Vijay froze?
qa.a: Abhinav was probably a little anxious for Vijay but calm, smiling so Vijay would feel safe.

qa.q: What helped Vijay settle with Rao uncle?
qa.a: Abhinav's calm smile and simple words showed Vijay the neighbour was safe, so he relaxed at his own pace.

qa.q: How might Rao uncle see Vijay pulling his moustache?
qa.a: He would probably feel delighted and warmly accepted by the little visitor.

grounding: It illustrates a visiting toddler held by neighbours unlike at home, who reads his father's comfort to decide how to react.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Keerthana, you look down when your teacher talks? Come, let your Kishore Thatha tell you. When I was nine, in Madurai, my father taught me never to stare into an elder's eyes. It was cheeky, he said. So when I went to the new mission school, I kept my eyes on my feet. Mr D'Costa, the English teacher, said, "Eyes up while I am speaking, boy." I couldn't. My neck would not lift. He thought I was hiding something. I thought he wanted me to be rude. I went home and cried. My father went with me the next morning. The two men talked for a long time. After that, Mr D'Costa would say, "Just look at my nose, Kishore." And my father said, "In his class, looking is listening." Both were right, you see.

qa.q: Where did Kishore go to school when he was nine?
qa.a: To the new mission school in Madurai.

qa.q: How did young Kishore feel when Mr D'Costa asked him to look up?
qa.a: He felt confused and upset, stuck between his father's rule and the teacher's request, and cried when he went home.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Thatha's story?
qa.a: His father going to the school the next morning to talk with Mr D'Costa, so both adults could explain their meanings to each other and to Kishore.

qa.q: How did Mr D'Costa first see Kishore's lowered eyes?
qa.a: He thought Kishore was hiding something, reading lowered eyes as dishonesty rather than respect.

grounding: It illustrates a child taught that meeting an elder's eyes is rude, who meets a teacher expecting eye contact and needs adults to translate.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Kalyani's first day at the school in Dubai was loud: a fire drill, a new timetable and thirty children talking at once. When Mr Vishal, the class teacher, asked her name, she answered to the floor, as she did with elders at home. "Kalyani, look at me when you speak," he said, quite kindly. The class went quiet. Kalyani felt her face burn. Looking at a teacher's eyes felt like talking back. She tried, but her eyes slid away to his watch. At pickup she told her mother, and her mother wrote a short note in her diary. The next day Mr Vishal crouched beside her desk. "In your family, looking down is polite, yes? Here, looking up helps me know you're listening. You can look at my chin to start." Kalyani tried his chin. It was easier.

qa.q: What did Mr Vishal suggest Kalyani could look at to start?
qa.a: He suggested she could look at his chin to start.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani's face burn when Mr Vishal asked her to look at him?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and uneasy, because at home looking into an elder's eyes felt like talking back, and the class had gone quiet.

qa.q: How did Mr Vishal support Kalyani?
qa.a: He explained both meanings, looking down at home and looking up in class, and gave her an easier first step of looking at his chin.

qa.q: How might Kalyani's mother have felt reading about the first day?
qa.a: She was probably concerned for Kalyani and wanted the teacher to understand, so she wrote a note to explain.

grounding: It illustrates a child raised to lower her eyes before elders who meets a teacher expecting eye contact, and the patient translation between the two.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Binita's Dadi had one rule she repeated at every visit: "Don't stare at elders, it's rude." So Binita, eight, looked at the floor when Dadi's friends spoke. In the new term at her Bengaluru school, Ojas sir took maths. On Monday he said, "Binita, eyes here, please," tapping his own eye. She lifted her face for a second, then dropped it. On Wednesday he said it again, more firmly. Binita's stomach knotted. Was she bad at home or bad at school? That evening she asked Dadi, who laughed softly. On Friday, Dadi wrote a note for Ojas sir. He read it, then knelt by her. "At home, lower eyes are respect. Here, looking at me tells me you're following. You're not being rude to anyone." Binita looked at him, just long enough to nod.

qa.q: What did Ojas sir tap when he said "eyes here, please"?
qa.a: He tapped his own eye.

qa.q: What was Binita worried about when Ojas sir asked again?
qa.a: She was anxious and confused, her stomach knotting, worried she was bad at home or bad at school.

qa.q: Which step helped most, and why?
qa.a: Dadi's note and Ojas sir kneeling to explain both meanings, because it showed Binita she was not being rude in either place.

qa.q: How might Ojas sir have seen Binita's lowered eyes at first?
qa.a: He may have thought she was not paying attention or was being shy, before the note helped him understand.

grounding: It illustrates a child taught that looking at elders is rude who meets a teacher asking for eye contact, and the patient translation between the two.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: Looking back on my exchange term in Munich, the moment I, Yamini, remember most is the soup. My host mother, Frau Weber, asked if I wanted more, and I said, "Maybe a little," the way I'd say it at home, meaning yes please. She put the pot away. I was shocked. And when my host sister Lena didn't want to come to the cinema with me and Aditi, the other Indian student, she just said, "No, I don't feel like it." No maybe, no excuse. I felt slapped. Aditi and I talked about it for an hour on the tram. At home, my mother says "we'll see" when she means no. Here "no" meant only no, and it wasn't cold. Lena still made me tea. By the end I was saying "Yes, please" and "No, thanks" like them, and it felt strangely light.

qa.q: What did Yamini say when asked if she wanted more soup?
qa.a: "Maybe a little."

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when Lena said a plain no?
qa.a: Yamini felt slapped and hurt at first, because at home a refusal is usually softened.

qa.q: What helped Yamini learn to read both styles?
qa.a: Talking it over with Aditi and noticing that Lena was still kind after saying no, which showed a blunt no was not rude there.

qa.q: How might Lena have seen Yamini's reaction to her plain no?
qa.a: Lena probably didn't notice any rudeness in it, and might have been puzzled if Yamini seemed hurt, since for her no is just honest.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager on exchange noticing blunt refusals abroad and softened ones at home, and learning to read both.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
Exchange coordinator's note, week 3, Utrecht programme.
Chetan asked to talk after the Tuesday session. He said his host mother, Sharmila, who moved to the Netherlands twenty years ago, and her Dutch husband keep saying no "straight to the face". When he offered to cook dinner, Sharmila said, "No, not tonight, I've planned something." When he asked to borrow the bicycle, the answer was "No, it has a flat tyre." Chetan said at home people would say "let's see" or "maybe tomorrow", and he'd been lying awake thinking the family didn't like him. He noticed Sharmila herself had changed; at an Indian dinner party she softened every refusal.
I explained that in this house a plain no is simply information, not a verdict. He laughed at himself a little. I suggested he ask Sharmila directly. He did, the same evening, and texted me: "She said she likes me a lot. Also she fixed the tyre."

qa.q: What reason did Sharmila give for saying no to the bicycle?
qa.a: "No, it has a flat tyre."

qa.q: How had Chetan been feeling about the family's plain answers?
qa.a: He had been anxious and hurt, lying awake thinking the family didn't like him.

qa.q: What did the coordinator suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To ask Sharmila directly, because a plain question matched the family's direct style and cleared up his worry the same evening.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see her own two ways of saying no?
qa.a: She probably moves between them without much thought, plain at home in Utrecht and softer at an Indian dinner party, and may have been surprised Chetan felt rejected.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager on exchange observing blunt refusals in his host family, contrasted with softened ones at home, and learning to read both.

passage:
Sunday night, Perth
Journal, today was weird. At the beach barbecue I asked Mia's dad if Saurabh could join us next weekend, and he said, "No, sorry, it's family only." Just that. Then he flipped a sausage like nothing happened. I stood there with my face burning. At home Papa would have said "we'll see, beta" and we'd all know it meant no, but softly.
Later Saurabh (who is staying with the Nguyens) said his host mum does the same. "Do you want dessert?" "No thanks." Done. He thinks it's efficient. I think it's a bit like being hit with a cushion. Not painful, just surprising.
But then Mia's dad asked me to choose the music for the car, as if nothing was wrong, because nothing was. Maybe here no is just no, and maybe at home maybe is also no. I'm learning two languages in English. Sarika, the translator.

qa.q: What did Mia's dad say when asked if Saurabh could join?
qa.a: "No, sorry, it's family only."

qa.q: How did Sarika feel when Mia's dad said no so plainly?
qa.a: Sarika was embarrassed and surprised, with a burning face, like being hit with a cushion.

qa.q: What is Sarika learning to do?
qa.a: Sarika is learning to read a blunt no as plain information here and a soft maybe as a no at home, without taking either as rude.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see the direct style?
qa.a: Saurabh sees it as efficient rather than rude, which helps Sarika think about it differently.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager on exchange noticing blunt refusals abroad and softened ones at home, and learning to read both as normal.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
Wednesday, Stockholm, 11 pm
Third week at the internship. Today at the coffee machine I was explaining my data slides to Erik, standing the way I'd stand with anyone in the Pune office, maybe an arm's length. He took a step back. I stepped forward, to keep talking. He stepped back again, into the bin. I felt my cheeks go hot. I thought, he doesn't like me, or I smell of the hostel's dal.
At lunch I sat alone and replayed it. Then Rajni, the senior analyst who moved here from Chennai years ago, sat with me and asked what was wrong. She laughed, gently. "People here like more space. Watch where they stand in the queue." I watched. There are gaps between everyone, even friends.
Tomorrow I'll stand a bit further back and see if Erik stops stepping. Indu, the space cadet.

qa.q: Where did Indu stand while explaining the slides to Erik?
qa.a: At the coffee machine, maybe an arm's length away, the way Indu would stand in the Pune office.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when Erik kept stepping back?
qa.a: Indu felt embarrassed and rejected, cheeks hot, and worried that Erik disliked Indu.

qa.q: What did Rajni suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She suggested watching where people stand in the queue, which lets Indu read local comfort distance and adjust.

qa.q: How might Erik have experienced the conversation at the coffee machine?
qa.a: Erik probably felt crowded and uncomfortable, not unfriendly, and kept stepping back to get the space he was used to.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult abroad who stands close to a colleague, feels rejected when they step back, and later learns about different comfort distances.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
The dairy co-operative in Moga had a visitor that month: Anouk, an agriculture trainer from the Netherlands, who worked alongside the staff. Alka, twenty, was chosen to translate for her. On the first morning, walking between the milk cans, Alka stood right at her shoulder, the way she and the other girls always stood, close enough to smell the tea. Anouk kept stepping sideways. By noon Alka felt hurt and foolish. Did she smell of cattle? Did she talk too much? She went quiet.
In the afternoon, Amandeep, the co-op supervisor, pulled her aside. "Her people keep a bigger gap. My cousin in Canada says the same about everyone there." Alka watched Anouk with the farmers after that: she kept about a stride away from all of them. The next day Alka stood a stride away too. Anouk smiled, and they talked for an hour.

qa.q: How far away did Anouk stand from the farmers?
qa.a: About a stride away.

qa.q: How did Alka feel by noon on the first day?
qa.a: Alka felt hurt and foolish, worrying she smelled of cattle or talked too much, and went quiet.

qa.q: What did Alka do that shows courtesy across cultures?
qa.a: She watched how Anouk stood with others, then adjusted her own distance to a stride, which let Anouk feel comfortable.

qa.q: How might Anouk have experienced the first morning?
qa.a: Anouk probably felt crowded and kept stepping sideways for comfort, perhaps without realising Alka felt rejected.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who stands close to a colleague from abroad, sees her step back and feels rejected, then learns about comfort distances and adjusts.
